OCR GCSE Religious Studies (J625) · J625/06 – Dialogue between religious and non-religious beliefs and attitudes
Mini-Lesson

Dialogue between religious and non-religious beliefs and attitudes

7 missions. Guess, learn, then check. Your place is saved.

  1. Mission 1Fewer than half of people in England and Wales now say they are Christian. Is Britain still Christian?
  2. Mission 2If you don't believe in God, where do your morals come from, and what happens when you die?
  3. Mission 3Faith schools, marriage, IVF, the right to die: where do religious and secular values clash?
  4. Mission 4Is a five-day-old embryo a person, a future person, or just a cluster of cells?
  5. Mission 5If someone is dying and in pain, is helping them die an act of mercy or of killing?
  6. Mission 6If you believe your religion is true, can you also believe other religions are true?
  7. Mission 7Can a believer and an atheist agree on how to live, and where do they part ways?
Mission 1

Mission 1: Fewer than half of people in England and Wales now say they are Christian. Is Britain still Christian?

Make a guess: Fewer than half of people in England and Wales now say they are Christian. Is Britain still Christian?

Mission 1

A Christian heritage

  • Christianity reached Britain under Roman rule. In 597, Augustine of Canterbury began a mission to the English.
  • For over 1,400 years Christianity shaped Britain's laws, calendar, language, art and buildings.
  • Parish churches and cathedrals stand in almost every town; many schools and hospitals were founded by churches.
  • You study this from the perspective of your chosen religion: notice how Christian heritage shapes the setting every British faith lives in.
Mission 1

Many traditions, one country

  • Christian traditions: Church of England (Anglican), Catholic, Methodist, Baptist, United Reformed, Pentecostal and black-majority churches, Orthodox, Quakers, Salvation Army.
  • Other religions: Islam, Hinduism, Sikhism, Judaism, Buddhism, and smaller groups.
  • Non-religious beliefs: atheism (the belief that there is no God) and Humanism (a non-religious approach to life based on reason and care for people).
  • Britain is mainly Christian in heritage and diverse in belief today.
Mission 1Read the source

Three censuses

The census asks "What is your religion?" (a voluntary question). England and Wales, % of all people:

200120112021
Christian71.759.346.2
No religion14.825.137.2
Muslim3.04.86.5
Hindu–1.51.7
  • Sikh, Jewish and Buddhist: each under 1% in 2011. About 7% did not answer the question.
  • Source: Office for National Statistics. Scotland and Northern Ireland hold separate censuses.

Q1 What changed in 2021 that had not happened before?

Show answer

Fewer than half said "Christian"; still the largest group.

Q2 Which two groups grew most from 2011 to 2021?

Show answer

No religion; Muslim.

Quick check
?Which conclusion does the 2021 census of England and Wales support?
Mission 1

The established Church

  • Established church: a church officially linked to the state by law.
  • The Church of England is the established church in England.
  • The Monarch is its Supreme Governor, and promises at the coronation to maintain it.
  • Parliament must approve some of its laws; the Monarch formally appoints its bishops and archbishops.
  • Not the whole UK: the Church in Wales was disestablished in 1920. The Church of Scotland is the national church but runs its own affairs. Northern Ireland has no established church.
  • Your spec: Christianity as the established religion in a country of diverse religious traditions.
Mission 1

Religion in public life

  • Bishops in the House of Lords: 26 Church of England bishops sit there (the "Lords Spiritual").
  • Christian services mark key events: coronations, royal weddings and funerals, Remembrance Sunday.
  • Public holidays based on Christian festivals: Christmas, Good Friday, Easter Monday (not in Scotland).
  • Church schools: many state schools are Church of England or Catholic.
  • Education Act 1988: RE must reflect that Britain's religious traditions are "in the main Christian" while taking account of other principal religions; school worship is to be mainly "broadly Christian".
  • Other traditions are recognised too: Eid, Diwali, Vaisakhi and Hanukkah celebrated in cities and at Downing Street; faith schools of other religions; chaplains of many faiths in hospitals, prisons and the armed forces.
Quick check
?Which of these is an example of the Church of England's established status?
Mission 1

Secularisation

  • Secularisation: religion losing influence over society, public life and people's lives.
  • Signs: falling church attendance; the rise of "no religion"; fewer religious weddings; laws changing away from church teaching.
  • The rise of humanism: more people live by non-religious values; Humanists UK (once the British Humanist Association) speaks for them.
  • Not the whole story: many people still pray, believe or call themselves Christian without attending. The sociologist Grace Davie called this "believing without belonging" (Religion in Britain since 1945, 1994).
  • Some churches are growing, especially Pentecostal, black-majority and immigrant congregations; other religions are growing too.
  • Your spec asks about the place of religion in a secular society and the effects of secularisation on religion.
Mission 1Diversity

Responding to a changing Britain

  • Church of England: serves every parish, believers or not; its leaders generally support remaining established so faith keeps a voice in public life.
  • Evangelical and Pentecostal churches: active mission, church planting, Alpha courses.
  • Other faiths: some leaders support establishment because it keeps a place for faith in public life; others ask for equal treatment of all beliefs.
  • Humanists UK and the National Secular Society: want a secular state: no established church, no bishops by right in the Lords, no religious selection in state schools.
  • The Sunday Assembly (founded in London, 2013): non-religious gatherings with songs, talks and community, without God.
Mission 1Evaluate

"Britain is no longer a Christian country."

  • Reasons for: fewer than half chose "Christian" in 2021; church attendance is low; many laws now differ from church teaching; Britain is diverse in religion and belief.
  • Reasons against: Christianity is still the largest group; laws, holidays and the calendar are rooted in Christianity; many people still believe without attending church.
  • Also against: the Church of England is still the established church, linked to the state by law.
  • Another view: "Christian" may describe heritage and culture rather than belief; Britain may be best described as diverse or plural (many faiths and beliefs side by side).
  • Judge it by: Does "Christian country" mean belief, practice, law or history? Which evidence counts most: census, attendance or public institutions?
Quick check
?Grace Davie described many British people as "believing without belonging". What does this mean?
Mission check

?A new town council plans its calendar. The council gives staff the Christmas Day bank holiday, opens with a prayer by the Anglican vicar, and also holds a Diwali lights event and an Eid reception. Which description of Britain does this best illustrate?

Britain's laws and calendar are rooted in Christianity, but its people are increasingly diverse, and many are non-religious.

Mission 2

Mission 2: If you don't believe in God, where do your morals come from, and what happens when you die?

Make a guess: If you don't believe in God, where do your morals come from, and what happens when you die?

Mission 2

Theist, atheist, agnostic

  • Theist: believes in God (or gods).
  • Atheist: believes there is no God (some atheists say simply that they lack belief in God).
  • Agnostic: believes we cannot know whether God exists, or has not decided. The word was coined by T. H. Huxley (1825–1895) in 1869.
  • These are answers to one question: does God exist?
  • Humanism goes further: a whole non-religious approach to life. Most Humanists are atheists or agnostics.
  • Secularism is different again: the view that the state should be neutral between beliefs. Many religious people are secularists.
Quick check
?Sam says: "There might be a God, there might not. I don't think anyone can know for sure." Which term best describes Sam?
Mission 2

What Humanists believe

  • Humanists see no good evidence for God or the supernatural; they understand the world through reason, evidence and science.
  • One life: there is no afterlife, so this life matters all the more.
  • Meaning is made, not given: people create purpose through relationships, work, learning and helping others.
  • Morality comes from people: reason, empathy and concern for human flourishing (wellbeing).
  • Humanists support human rights, equality and freedom of belief for everyone.
  • Groups: Humanists UK (Britain); Humanists International (Amsterdam Declaration, 2002).
Mission 2

How Humanists decide what is right

  • Ask: What are the consequences? Who is helped, who is harmed?
  • Empathy: treat others as you would want to be treated (the Golden Rule, found in many cultures).
  • Respect for choice: people should run their own lives if they harm no one else.
  • Examples: many Humanists support legal assisted dying, a woman's right to choose on abortion, and equal marriage.
  • Humanists hold non-religious ceremonies: weddings, naming ceremonies, funerals.
  • Humanists do not all agree: each person must think the issue through.
Quick check
?A Humanist is deciding whether to give a kidney to a stranger. Which line of reasoning is most typically Humanist?
Mission 2Diversity

Shared values and disagreements

  • Shared: human dignity and rights; care for the vulnerable; honesty; justice; freedom of belief.
  • Disagree about: where morality comes from (God or humans); life after death; assisted dying and abortion; faith schools; bishops in the House of Lords.
  • Dialogue means understanding each other's reasons, not winning.
  • More on dialogue between religious and non-religious worldviews.
Mission 2Evaluate

"You can be a good person without believing in God."

  • Reasons for: many atheists and Humanists live honest, generous lives; empathy and reason can guide action; Paul says Gentiles without the Jewish law can show "the work of the law written in their hearts" (Romans 2:15), and some Christians apply this to non-believers.
  • Reasons against: many believers argue that without God there is no objective standard of goodness (one that holds whatever anyone thinks); religion gives motivation, community and forgiveness; Catholic teaching sees moral law as rooted in God, even when people do not know it.
  • Another view: many religious people agree non-believers can act well, but say true goodness includes loving God.
  • Judge it by: What does "good" mean: acting well, or a relationship with God? Must a standard be objective to be real?
Mission check

?At a hospital ethics meeting, a Humanist and a Catholic both oppose a plan to cut care for elderly patients. Which statement best describes their positions?

Non-religious people build ethics on reason and empathy; they often reach the same actions as believers, for different reasons.

Mission 3

Mission 3: Faith schools, marriage, IVF, the right to die: where do religious and secular values clash?

Make a guess: Faith schools, marriage, IVF, the right to die: where do religious and secular values clash?

Mission 3

Two sources of values

  • Secular values: based on human reason and agreement, not on religion: freedom of choice (self-determination), equality, avoiding harm.
  • Religious values: based on God's will, scripture, tradition and conscience: e.g. the sanctity of life, marriage as sacred.
  • In a secular society, law is made for everyone, of every faith and none.
  • Clashes happen when the law allows what a religion forbids, or requires what a religion rejects.
  • You answer from the perspective of your chosen religion: notice how your tradition responds, and how its members differ.
Mission 3

Values in school

  • Secular ethics in school: respect, equality and personal choice; science teaches evolution; Relationships and Sex Education is compulsory (since 2020).
  • Education Reform Act 1988: every state school must teach RE and hold daily collective worship; parents may withdraw their children.
  • Faith schools (with a religious character) teach the national curriculum, plus RE and worship in their own tradition. RSE may be taught in line with their faith's teachings.
  • For: parents' right to raise children in their faith; strong values and community; often popular and successful.
  • Against (e.g. Humanists UK): selecting pupils by religion can divide communities; state money should not fund religious teaching.
Mission 3Diversity

Faith schools across traditions

  • Christian: most faith schools are Church of England or Catholic. Catholic teaching: parents are the first educators; schools help pass on the faith.
  • Jewish: many Jewish schools (Orthodox and progressive) teach Hebrew and Torah alongside the curriculum.
  • Muslim: state-funded Muslim schools since 1998, and many independent ones; Muslims value learning ("seek knowledge") within Islamic values.
  • Hindu: Krishna Avanti Primary School, Harrow (2008), was the first state-funded Hindu school.
  • Buddhist: very few Buddhist schools; many Buddhists stress the Kalama Sutta: test teachings by experience, not just tradition.
  • Clash points: admissions by faith; teaching about relationships and sexuality; dress; time for prayer and festivals.
Quick check
?Which is a clash between religious and secular values in education?
Mission 3

Marriage and the law

  • Arranged marriage: families help choose a partner, but both freely consent. Legal and common in many Hindu, Sikh, Muslim and some Jewish families.
  • Forced marriage: one or both do not consent. A crime in England and Wales since 2014.
  • Child marriage: since 2023 no one under 18 may marry in England and Wales, even with parents' consent.
  • Every major religion in Britain teaches that marriage needs free consent: Catholic teaching says a marriage made under force is not valid; Islam requires the bride's consent; the Sikh Rahit Maryada forbids child marriage; Hindu and Jewish leaders condemn forced marriage.
  • Clash points: some religious weddings (e.g. many Islamic nikahs) are not legally registered, leaving spouses without legal protection; same-sex marriage (next screen).
Mission 3

Equality laws

  • Equality Act 2010: it is illegal to discriminate because of nine protected characteristics, including religion or belief, sex and sexual orientation.
  • Exemptions: religions may choose ministers by their own rules (e.g. only men as Catholic priests).
  • Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013: same-sex marriage is legal, but no religious group is forced to hold such weddings; the Church of England is barred unless it changes its own rules.
  • Court cases under equality law: a Christian B&B was found to have unlawfully refused a double room to a gay couple (2013). But a Christian bakery in Belfast could refuse to ice a slogan backing same-sex marriage: the Supreme Court said that was about the message, not the customer (2018).
  • Views divide within religions: some believers welcome equality laws as justice; others ask for wider freedom of conscience.
Quick check
?In the 2018 "Ashers bakery" case, why did the UK Supreme Court rule in favour of the Christian bakers?
Mission 3

Abortion and euthanasia

  • Law: abortion is legal under the Abortion Act 1967 (usually up to 24 weeks, with two doctors' agreement). Assisting suicide is a crime (Suicide Act 1961), though Parliament has been debating a law on assisted dying for the terminally ill.
  • Christian: "You formed my inmost being. You knit me together in my mother's womb." (Psalm 139:13); "You shall not murder" (Exodus 20:13). the Catholic Church teaches that abortion and euthanasia are always wrong; the Church of England accepts abortion in strictly limited cases; SPUC campaigns for unborn life.
  • Muslim: "whoso saveth the life of one, it shall be as if he had saved the life of all mankind" (Surah 5:32, Pickthall); life is Allah's (17:33; 4:29). Many scholars allow abortion before ensoulment (120 days) for serious reasons; euthanasia is widely forbidden.
  • Jewish: Exodus 21:22–25 treats harm to an unborn child less gravely than killing a person, so the mother's life comes first. Euthanasia is forbidden, but needless prolonging of dying may be withdrawn.
  • Buddhist: the First Precept (do not harm life) and ahimsa. The Vakkali and Channa Suttas, where gravely ill monks end their lives, are read in different ways.
  • Hindu: ahimsa; the Garbha Upanishad describes the self as present in the womb, so many Hindus oppose abortion.
Mission 3

Genetic manipulation and creating life

  • Law: the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Acts (1990, 2008) allow regulated IVF, embryo research up to 14 days, embryo screening and (since 2015) mitochondrial donation. Reproductive cloning and editing embryos for birth are banned.
  • "Playing God?" Some believers say creating or changing life oversteps God's role; others say healing is God's work done through science.
  • Catholic: opposes IVF that separates conception from the couple's union, and research that destroys embryos; supports gene therapy to heal patients. Anglican: accepts IVF and limited embryo research.
  • Muslim: IVF allowed within marriage using the couple's own eggs and sperm. Jewish: IVF generally welcomed ("be fruitful"); saving life (pikuach nefesh) supports medical research.
  • Buddhist: judged by intention and harm. Hindu: many accept IVF within marriage; views on embryo research vary.
Quick check
?Which statement about UK law and medical ethics is correct?
Mission 3Evaluate

"Religious beliefs should never shape the law in a secular society."

  • Reasons for: laws apply to people of every belief and none; religious rules should not be forced on others; reason and evidence are shared by all; secular law protects minority faiths too.
  • Reasons against: many laws (e.g. against murder and theft) share roots with religious ethics; believers are citizens with a right to argue from their values; religions defend the vulnerable (e.g. the unborn, the dying); freedom of religion needs protection in law.
  • Other views: religious arguments should be translated into reasons others can accept; exemptions can balance conscience and equality.
  • Judge it by: Whose freedom is at stake? Can a law be neutral? Should believers be allowed to opt out?
Mission check

?A hospital nurse is asked to take part in an abortion, which her faith teaches is wrong. UK law lets her refuse to take part directly. Which idea does this exemption best show?

Clashes between religious and secular values happen in schools, marriage law and medicine; the law often tries to balance equality and freedom of conscience.

Mission 4

Mission 4: Is a five-day-old embryo a person, a future person, or just a cluster of cells?

Make a guess: Is a five-day-old embryo a person, a future person, or just a cluster of cells?

Mission 4

From fertilisation to fourteen days

  • Fertilisation: egg and sperm join to form a single cell, the zygote, with a full set of human DNA.
  • Day 5–6: a hollow ball of about 100–200 cells, the blastocyst. This is when IVF embryos are usually transferred or frozen.
  • Days 6–12: implantation in the lining of the womb.
  • About day 14: the primitive streak appears, the first sign of the body's head-to-tail axis; the nervous system starts to form soon after. After this the embryo can no longer split into twins.
  • From about 8 weeks it is called a foetus.
  • Embryo: the early stage of development, from fertilisation to about 8 weeks.
Mission 4

What is the status of an embryo?

  • A person from conception: a new human life with its own DNA; it must be protected like any person (Catholic teaching; many evangelicals; many Buddhists, who hold that consciousness begins at conception).
  • A potential person: it deserves special respect, but not the full rights of a born child (e.g. the Warnock Report, 1984; many Anglicans).
  • Gradual: its value grows as it develops, e.g. after the primitive streak, or when the heart or brain forms.
  • A cluster of cells: with no brain and no feelings, it is not yet "someone" (some Humanists and philosophers).
  • Ensoulment: many Muslims hold that the soul is breathed in at 120 days (some say 40); many Jews follow the Talmud that before 40 days the embryo is "like water"; many Hindus believe the atman is present from conception (the Garbha Upanishad traces life from conception).
Mission 4Read the source

Known before birth

"For you formed my inmost being. You knit me together in my mother's womb." (Psalm 139:13)

"Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you. Before you were born, I sanctified you." (Jeremiah 1:5)

  • "You shall not murder." (Exodus 20:13)

Q1 What do these verses suggest about God and life before birth?

Show answer

God knows, forms and values each person from the very start.

Q2 Why do some Christians say they do not settle the status of an IVF embryo?

Show answer

They are poetry about a pregnancy in the womb, not rules about embryos in a lab.

Quick check
?Why does the primitive streak, at about 14 days, matter in the debate about embryos?
Mission 4

Genetic manipulation and "creating life"

  • Gene therapy: repairing faulty genes. Somatic (body cells): affects only the patient. Germline (eggs, sperm, embryos): passed to future generations; illegal for reproduction in the UK.
  • Embryo screening (PGD): testing IVF embryos for serious inherited conditions and choosing a healthy one; "saviour siblings" chosen to match a sick brother or sister.
  • Designer babies: choosing traits like looks or intelligence: not allowed, but feared.
  • Mitochondrial donation: replaces faulty mitochondria with a donor's; legal in the UK since 2015.
  • Cloning: Dolly the sheep (1996). Reproductive human cloning is banned in the UK.
  • Creating life: making new life in the lab (IVF, cloning, synthetic cells). Critics call it "playing God"; supporters call it using God-given skill.
Mission 4

Christian responses

  • Catholic: the embryo is to be treated as a person from conception, so no research that destroys embryos, no embryo selection, no cloning. Somatic gene therapy and adult stem-cell research are welcomed.
  • Many Anglicans and other Protestants: research up to 14 days can be right if it may relieve great suffering, with the embryo treated with special respect.
  • "Playing God": only God gives life; changing the human germline crosses a line.
  • "Co-creators": humans are made in God's image and given skill and stewardship (Genesis 1:28); healing is Christ-like.
  • Denominations differ: Catholic and many evangelical Christians oppose embryo destruction; many liberal Protestants accept regulated research.
Mission 4Diversity

Other religions and Humanists

  • Islam: "whoso saveth the life of one, it shall be as if he had saved the life of all mankind" (Qur'an 5:32, Pickthall): used to support research that may cure. Many scholars allow research on early spare embryos (before ensoulment), but not altering God's creation for trivial reasons.
  • Life is sacred: "slay not the life which Allah hath forbidden save with right" (Qur'an 17:33); "kill not one another" (Qur'an 4:29).
  • Judaism: saving life (pikuach nefesh) is a great duty; many authorities support embryo research and screening.
  • Buddhism: the First Precept (not harming living beings) leads many to oppose destroying embryos; compassion leads others to accept research.
  • Hinduism: ahimsa (non-violence) and the belief that the atman is present from conception lead many to oppose destroying embryos; others stress relieving suffering.
  • Humanists: decide by evidence and outcomes: support regulated research and screening to reduce suffering; oppose designer babies.
Quick check
?A Catholic and an Anglican both read Psalm 139:13 ("You knit me together in my mother's womb"). Which statement fits their likely positions on embryo research?
Mission 4Evaluate

"Scientists who change human embryos are playing God."

  • Reasons for: only God gives life; germline changes affect people not yet born; risk of designer babies; destroyed embryos may be human lives.
  • Sources for: Psalm 139:13; Exodus 20:13.
  • Also for: the First Precept; ahimsa.
  • Reasons against: curing disease is a duty; humans are stewards and co-creators; Humanists: the phrase assumes a God; outcomes and consent matter.
  • Sources against: Qur'an 5:32; pikuach nefesh.
  • Another view: some changes (preventing a deadly disease) may be right while others (choosing looks) are not.
  • Judge it by: Where does healing end and "enhancement" begin? Whose consent counts? Does the embryo's status decide everything?
Mission check

?A scientist agrees to research on embryos that are 10 days old, but refuses to use embryos that are 20 days old. Which belief best explains this line?

Where you draw the line on embryos depends on when you believe a person, or a soul, begins.

Mission 5

Mission 5: If someone is dying and in pain, is helping them die an act of mercy or of killing?

Make a guess: If someone is dying and in pain, is helping them die an act of mercy or of killing?

Mission 5

Kinds of euthanasia

  • Euthanasia (Greek: "good death"): ending a life to relieve suffering, sometimes called mercy killing.
  • Voluntary: the person asks for it. Non-voluntary: the person cannot ask (e.g. in a long-term coma). Involuntary: against, or without asking, the wishes of a person who could decide.
  • Active: something is done to end life (e.g. a lethal injection). Passive: treatment that keeps someone alive is withdrawn or withheld, and they die of their illness.
  • Assisted suicide (assisted dying): the person ends their own life with help, e.g. with drugs prescribed by a doctor.
  • Not euthanasia: refusing treatment that is too burdensome, or giving pain relief that may shorten life when the aim is to ease pain.
Mission 5

The law

  • UK: active euthanasia is treated as murder or manslaughter. In England and Wales, assisting suicide is a crime (Suicide Act 1961).
  • Withdrawing treatment that is no longer in a patient's best interests can be lawful (e.g. the Tony Bland case, 1993). Patients may refuse treatment.
  • In 2025 MPs voted for a bill to allow assisted dying for some terminally ill adults in England and Wales, but it ran out of time in the House of Lords in 2026 and did not become law. The Scottish Parliament rejected a similar bill in March 2026.
  • Elsewhere: euthanasia is legal in the Netherlands and Belgium (2002) and Canada (2016); assisted suicide is allowed in Switzerland and some US states (Oregon, 1997).
Quick check
?A man with motor neurone disease, who is fully able to decide, asks his doctor for a lethal injection, and the doctor gives it. What kind of euthanasia is this?
Mission 5Diversity

Christian views

  • Catholic teaching (Catechism of the Catholic Church 2276–2279, paraphrase): direct euthanasia, whatever the motive, is murder and gravely wrong. Stopping treatment that is burdensome, extraordinary or disproportionate can be right. Painkillers may be given even if they may shorten life, if death is not intended. Palliative care is a special form of charity.
  • Church of England and most other churches oppose changing the law: life is God's gift; vulnerable people could feel pressure to die.
  • Some Christians support assisted dying out of compassion; e.g. a former Archbishop of Canterbury, Lord Carey (2014), and Archbishop Desmond Tutu.
Mission 5Diversity

Islam and Judaism

  • Islam: "No soul can ever die except by Allah's leave and at a term appointed" (Qur'an 3:145, Pickthall). Life is a test; euthanasia and assisted suicide are forbidden.
  • Surahs 5:32, 17:33 ("slay not the life which Allah hath forbidden save with right", Pickthall) and 4:29 ("kill not one another") are used against euthanasia.
  • Many Muslim scholars allow switching off life support when treatment is futile; hospice care is supported.
  • Judaism: life belongs to God; even a dying person (goses) must not have death hastened.
  • But it may be right to remove something that holds back death without benefit (a traditional example: stopping a woodchopper's noise that keeps a dying man from dying).
  • Orthodox Jews oppose euthanasia; some Reform Jews accept assisted dying with safeguards. Most support hospice care.
Mission 5Diversity

Hinduism, Sikhism, Buddhism

  • Hinduism: ahimsa; ending life early may disturb the atman's journey and bring bad karma, for patient and doctor.
  • Some Hindus argue that relieving suffering is a duty (compassion), and traditional texts allow prayopavesa (fasting to death) for some elderly people in rare cases.
  • Sikhism: life is God's gift; birth and death are by hukam (God's will). Most Sikhs oppose euthanasia and stress sewa: caring for the sick.
  • Buddhism: the First Precept; the state of mind at death affects rebirth. Most Buddhists do not approve of euthanasia.
  • Vakkali Sutta: a monk in great pain takes his own life; the Buddha says he reached final nirvana.
  • The Channa Sutta tells a similar story.
  • Most Buddhists say these accounts concern enlightened beings, not a model for others.
Mission 5Evaluate

"Euthanasia should be legal in the UK."

  • Reasons for: autonomy (Humanists; Dignity in Dying, a UK campaign group); compassion (Christian agape, Buddhist karuna); quality of life; strict safeguards work in other countries.
  • Reasons against: sanctity of life (Job 1:21); vulnerable people may feel a burden; the slippery slope; good palliative care (hospices) relieves most suffering; doctors are meant to heal.
  • Other traditions add Qur'an 3:145, the First Precept and ahimsa.
  • Middle positions: allow refusing treatment and strong pain relief, but not active euthanasia (Catholic and many other teachings).
  • Judge it by: Whose life is it? Can safeguards protect the vulnerable? Is relieving suffering the same as ending life?
Mission check

?A hospice nurse, a practising Catholic, cares for a dying patient who says: "I just want the pain to stop." Which response best fits her faith and her work?

Almost everyone agrees that suffering should be relieved; the disagreement is whether this may ever include deliberately ending a life.

Mission 6

Mission 6: If you believe your religion is true, can you also believe other religions are true?

Make a guess: If you believe your religion is true, can you also believe other religions are true?

Mission 6

Three answers

  • Exclusivism: only one religion is true and leads to salvation. Many evangelical Christians cite "I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me." (John 14:6)
  • Inclusivism: one religion holds the fullest truth, but people of other faiths may share in it. The Catholic Church "rejects nothing that is true and holy" in other religions (Nostra Aetate 2, 1965).
  • Pluralism: many religions are valid paths to the same ultimate reality. Philosopher John Hick (1922–2012) argued this in God and the Universe of Faiths (1973).
  • Each religion contains people who hold each view.
Mission 6Read the source

Other faiths in scripture

"There is no compulsion in religion." (Surah 2:256, Pickthall)

"Lo! those who believe, and those who are Jews, and Sabaeans, and Christians - Whosoever believeth in Allah and the Last Day and doeth right - there shall no fear come upon them neither shall they grieve." (Surah 5:69, Pickthall)

  • Rig Veda 1.164.46: "Truth is one; the wise call it by many names" (paraphrase).
  • Bhagavad Gita 4.11: Krishna says he receives people by whatever path they come, for "all men everywhere / Shall fall into my path" (Arnold).

Q1 Which verse forbids forcing anyone to accept a religion?

Show answer

Surah 2:256.

Q2 Which two sources would support a pluralist view?

Show answer

Rig Veda 1.164.46; Bhagavad Gita 4.11.

Mission 6

How each tradition sees other faiths

  • Christianity: all three views are held. Most agree all people must be loved (Matthew 22:37–40).
  • Islam: Jews and Christians are "People of the Book". The Constitution of Madinah (622) made Muslims, Jews and others of Madinah one community for defence, each keeping its religion.
  • Judaism: non-Jews need not convert: those who keep the seven Noachide laws are righteous. Reconstructionist Judaism rejects the idea that Jews are chosen above others.
  • Buddhism: the Dhamma is tested by experience; the Dalai Lama argues for real respect between faiths while each keeps its own (Towards the True Kinship of Faiths, 2010).
  • Hinduism: many Hindus are pluralist or inclusivist (Rig Veda 1.164.46); some stress that only true knowledge (vidya) frees from samsara.
  • Sikhism: Guru Nanak taught there is one God of all.
Quick check
?A Christian says: "Jesus is the fullest truth, but God's grace can reach a sincere Muslim through her prayer." Which view is this?
Mission 6

Dialogue within a religion

  • Ecumenism: Christian churches working towards unity: Jesus prayed "that they may all be one" (John 17:21).
  • Examples: World Council of Churches (1948); Churches Together in England (1990); the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity (18–25 January).
  • Intra-faith communication: dialogue between groups in one religion: Sunni and Shi'a Muslims; Orthodox, Reform and Liberal Jews (the Board of Deputies of British Jews speaks for many); Theravada and Mahayana Buddhists; Hindu groups through umbrella bodies.
  • Aim: unity, shared action and fewer misunderstandings, without pretending differences do not exist.
Mission 6

Inter-faith dialogue in Britain

  • Inter-faith dialogue: people of different religions meeting to understand, respect and work with each other.
  • Four forms: dialogue of life (neighbours), of action (working together), of theological exchange, of religious experience (sharing prayer and silence).
  • Examples: Council of Christians and Jews (1942); Christian Muslim Forum (2006); Hindu Christian Forum UK; local inter-faith councils; Inter Faith Week each November.
  • Why it matters in 21st-century Britain: a multi-faith society; fighting prejudice and extremism; joint work on poverty and the environment; responding together after attacks or disasters.
Mission 6

The Catholic Church and dialogue

  • Nostra Aetate (1965): Catholics should respect other religions and work with their followers. Dignitatis Humanae (1965): every person has a right to religious freedom.
  • Pope John Paul II invited leaders of many religions to pray for peace at Assisi (1986). Pope Francis and the Grand Imam of al-Azhar signed the Document on Human Fraternity (2019).
  • Catholics hold dialogue and proclamation together: respect for others, while still sharing the Gospel.
Quick check
?Which document of the Second Vatican Council is the basis of Catholic inter-faith dialogue?
Mission 6

Proselytisation

  • Proselytisation: trying to convert others to your religion.
  • Christianity: "Go and make disciples of all nations" (Matthew 28:19). Evangelism shares the Gospel freely (e.g. the Alpha course); most Churches reject pressure or bribes.
  • Islam: da'wah (invitation to Islam): "Call unto the way of thy Lord with wisdom and fair exhortation" (Surah 16:125, Pickthall), never by force: "There is no compulsion in religion." (Surah 2:256, Pickthall)
  • Judaism accepts converts but does not seek them. Sikhs do not seek converts. Most Hindus do not, though ISKCON shares its teaching widely. Buddhists share the Dhamma when asked.
  • Religion and national identity: the Church of England and Englishness; Sikh and Punjabi identity; British Jewish and Muslim communities: faith can unite a nation, or make some feel outsiders.
  • Criticism: Humanists and others say pressing beliefs on people disrespects them. UK law protects the freedom to change religion (Human Rights Act 1998, Article 9).
Quick check
?Which teaching would a Muslim give against forcing someone to convert?
Mission 6Evaluate

"Religious people should not try to convert others."

  • Reasons for: pressure disrespects others' freedom and beliefs; it can damage community relations; pluralists see no need; dialogue builds understanding better.
  • Reasons against: if you believe something is true and saving, sharing it is love; Matthew 28:19 and da'wah are commands; freedom of speech includes religious speech; people remain free to say no.
  • Other views: share by example, not argument; answer questions honestly when asked; never use force, bribes or deception.
  • Judge it by: Is there a difference between inviting and pressuring? Does respect mean silence?
Mission check

?At an inter-faith week event, a Hindu speaker says: "God is one, and the different religions are like rivers flowing into the same sea." Which view does this express?

Believers answer the question in different ways: exclusivist, inclusivist or pluralist, and all three views are found in most religions.

Mission 7

Mission 7: Can a believer and an atheist agree on how to live, and where do they part ways?

Make a guess: Can a believer and an atheist agree on how to live, and where do they part ways?

Mission 7

Four non-religious positions

  • Atheism: the belief that there is no God.
  • Agnosticism: the view that we do not, or cannot, know whether God exists.
  • Humanism: a non-religious way of life built on reason, evidence, empathy and human flourishing. In Britain, Humanists UK (called the British Humanist Association until 2017) speaks for it.
  • Secularism: the view that the state and public institutions should be neutral between religions and beliefs. The National Secular Society (founded 1866) campaigns for it.
  • Say: secularism is about the state, not about personal belief. Many religious people are secularists.
  • Your spec calls these "non-religious worldviews". You answer from the perspective of the religion you study.
Mission 7

Values held in common

  • Human dignity: every person has worth. Religions ground this in God (or in the shared capacity for awakening); Humanists ground it in human nature and empathy.
  • The golden rule: treat others as you would want to be treated. Jesus: "whatever you desire for men to do to you, you shall also do to them" (Matthew 7:12).
  • Justice and equality: fair treatment, care for the poor, opposing discrimination.
  • Freedom of belief: "There is no compulsion in religion." (Qur'an 2:256, Pickthall)
  • Honesty, compassion, care for the planet.
  • Significance: for individuals, friendship across belief; for communities, joint food banks, refugee support, interfaith-and-belief forums; for society, shared laws on human rights.
Quick check
?A Christian vicar says she is a secularist. Which statement best explains how this is possible?
Mission 7

Where they part ways

  • Where morals come from: God's revelation and commands, or reason, evidence and empathy alone.
  • What a human is: a soul made by God (or a being in samsara), or a product of evolution with one life.
  • Life after death: judgement, heaven, rebirth or liberation; most Humanists believe death is the end.
  • Value of life: sanctity of life (life is sacred, given by God) versus quality of life and personal choice, e.g. assisted dying and abortion.
  • Religion in public life: bishops in the House of Lords, faith schools, daily collective worship in schools. Humanists UK and the National Secular Society campaign to change these; many religious groups defend them.
  • Significance: individuals may face clashes of conscience; communities may disagree over schools; society must decide whose values shape law.
Mission 7Diversity

Christian, Muslim and Jewish responses

  • Christian: many Christians welcome shared work for the common good: love of neighbour (Matthew 22:37–40) is for all. Catholic teaching holds that all people can know basic moral law by reason, so dialogue is natural. Some evangelicals stress that without Christ people cannot be saved, so they share their faith. "In my Father's house are many homes" (John 14:2) is read by some as hope for non-believers too.
  • Muslim: freedom of belief (2:256) supports peaceful coexistence and many Muslims value a secular state that protects their practice. Most Muslims hold that God's guidance comes before human values when the two truly conflict.
  • Jewish: Torah im Derech Eretz (Torah with "the way of the land"), the approach of Rabbi Samson Raphael Hirsch (1808–1888): keep Torah fully while taking part in wider society. The Board of Deputies of British Jews works with government and other groups. Some Jews are secular or Humanistic; Reform and Liberal Jews tend to embrace secular values more readily than many Orthodox Jews.
Mission 7Diversity

Buddhist and Hindu responses

  • Buddhist: Buddhism has no creator God, so it shares much with atheism and Humanism: no blind faith, ethics based on reducing suffering.
  • The Kalama Sutta (paraphrase): do not accept a teaching just because of tradition, scripture or a teacher; accept it when you know for yourself it is wholesome and leads to welfare.
  • The Insight Meditation Society (Massachusetts, 1975) aims, in your spec's words, to present Buddhism "without the complications of rituals, robes, chanting and the whole religious tradition".
  • Secular Buddhism (e.g. Stephen Batchelor, b. 1953) keeps practice but sets aside rebirth. Many traditional Theravada and Mahayana Buddhists disagree: kamma and rebirth are central teachings.
  • Hindu: most Hindus believe in Brahman (ultimate reality), and many worship Ishvara (a personal God). But Hindu thought includes non-theist schools, and the ancient Charvaka school rejected gods and an afterlife.
  • Shared values: the yamas (e.g. ahimsa, non-violence; satya, truthfulness). Disagreements: maya (illusion) and avidya (ignorance) mean that, for Hindus, a purely material view of life misses the truth (vidya).
Quick check
?Which Buddhist source is most often used to show that Buddhism encourages testing teachings rather than accepting them on authority?
Mission 7Read the source

Obeying God and the Prophet

"O ye who believe! Obey Allah, and obey the messenger and those of you who are in authority; …" (Qur'an 4:59, Pickthall)

"Verily in the messenger of Allah ye have a good example for him who looketh unto Allah and the Last Day, and remembereth Allah much." (Qur'an 33:21, Pickthall)

  • Shari'ah (the "path" or way): God's guidance for the whole of life, drawn from the Qur'an and the Prophet's example (Sunnah).

Q1 Who must Muslims obey, according to 4:59?

Show answer

Allah, the messenger, and those in authority.

Q2 Why does 33:21 matter for Shari'ah?

Show answer

The Prophet's life is the model, so his example shows how to live the Qur'an.

Mission 7

"You don't need religious rules to be good"

  • The non-religious argument (atheist, Humanist): people can be good using reason and empathy; rituals such as prayer and fasting change nothing; rules from the 7th century do not fit modern life; state law already protects people.
  • Muslim responses:
  • Shari'ah is not only about being good to others. Ibadah (worship) is the purpose of life: "I created the jinn and humankind only that they might worship Me." (Qur'an 51:56, Pickthall)
  • The Creator knows what is best for people, so God's guidance is wiser than any human system.
  • Prayer and fasting train self-discipline and God-consciousness (taqwa), and build the ummah (community).
  • Many British Muslims see no clash: following the law of the land is itself part of keeping agreements, and much of Shari'ah is personal (prayer, food, charity, finance).
  • Muslims differ: the Sunni schools of law and Shi'a (Ja'fari) law reach different rulings; some modern Muslims stress the purposes (maqasid) of Shari'ah over its detailed rules.
Quick check
?A Humanist argues that fasting in Ramadan is unnecessary because it does not make anyone a better person. Which response would most Muslims (Sunni and Shi'a) be most likely to give?
Mission 7Evaluate

"Secular values should take precedence over religious values."

  • Reasons for: in a diverse society, laws must be based on reasons everyone can share, not one faith's scripture. Secular law protects religious minorities too. Secular values such as equality have protected groups that some religious teachings have treated unfairly.
  • Reasons against: many religious people believe God's will is higher than any human law (Acts 5:29: obey God rather than people, paraphrase). Many shared values (dignity, care for the poor) grew from religious traditions. Secular values can also change with fashion or majority opinion.
  • Middle views: many believers accept secular law in public while following religious values in private; Hirsch's Torah im Derech Eretz; Muslim scholars who teach keeping the law of the land.
  • Judge it by: Does "secular" mean neutral or anti-religious? Who decides when values clash? Is there a difference between law and personal morality?
Mission check

?A hospital in Britain is planning its chaplaincy team. A Humanist proposes that a non-religious pastoral carer should join the Christian, Muslim, Jewish and Hindu chaplains. Which statement best describes the shared value and the disagreement here?

Dialogue works when both sides name what they share and are honest about where they differ.

Recap

The big ideas

Mission 1

  • Christianity is Britain's main religious tradition in history and culture; Britain is diverse in religion and non-religious belief.
  • Census (England and Wales): Christian 72% (2001) → 59% (2011) → 46% (2021); no religion 15% → 25% → 37%.
  • The Church of England is established; religion remains in public life, while secularisation reduces its influence.

Mission 2

  • Theist: believes in God; atheist: believes there is no God; agnostic: cannot know.
  • Humanists: no God, one life, ethics from reason, empathy and human flourishing.

Mission 3

  • Secular values stress choice, equality and avoiding harm; religious values stress God's will and the sanctity of life.
  • Clashes: faith schools; forced and child marriage (all religions require consent); equality law exemptions; abortion, euthanasia, IVF and genetics.
  • Each religion responds differently, and believers within each tradition disagree.

Mission 4

  • Views on the embryo: a person from conception, a potential person, gradual value, or a cluster of cells.
  • Genetic manipulation (gene therapy, screening, mitochondrial donation, cloning) divides religious believers between "playing God" and using God-given skill to heal.

Mission 5

  • Euthanasia: voluntary, non-voluntary, involuntary; active or passive; assisted suicide. In the UK active euthanasia and assisting suicide are crimes; bills to allow assisted dying failed in 2026.
  • Most religions oppose euthanasia (sanctity of life, God decides, karma, First Precept) and support hospices and palliative care (Cicely Saunders, 1967); Catholic teaching allows refusing burdensome treatment and strong pain relief.
  • Humanists and Dignity in Dying support assisted dying for autonomy and quality of life; utilitarianism may support it; some non-religious groups oppose it.

Mission 6

  • Exclusivism: one true religion. Inclusivism: one fullest truth others can share. Pluralism: many paths to one reality.
  • Ecumenism (within Christianity), intra-faith and inter-faith dialogue build understanding in multi-faith Britain.
  • Proselytisation divides opinion: sharing truth, or disrespecting freedom?

Mission 7

  • Atheism, agnosticism and Humanism are views about God and life; secularism is a view about the state.
  • Religions share many values with non-religious people (dignity, golden rule, justice, freedom of belief) but differ on the source of morality, life after death, the value of life and religion's place in public life.
  • Many Muslims answer "you don't need religious rules" by saying observance is worship of God, not only good behaviour.
